title: Jeff Nippard's Push Pull Legs program review
summary: NH reviews the publicly available version of Jeff Nippard's hypertrophy PPL day by day. He finds the push days solid, the leg day decent, and the pull days the weakest, since they have no deadlift and too much lat and isolation fluff. He suggests reordering the days, spreading calf work, adding long-head triceps work and using supersets.
claims: Push-pull-legs run in that order is the worst version of the template: a proper pull day fatigues the legs before squats
Opening push day with bench 4x4-6 at RPE 7-8 is a good strength hook; the narrow rep range means some sandbagging, which is fine
Incline cable fly 3x12-15 is a good chest finisher; some people get a good upper chest contraction from it, others do not
Standing dumbbell press can be done seated; it makes little difference and 4x10-12 complements the bench well
After two presses the front delts are fully worked, so lateral raises for the side and rear delts make sense
Face pulls at the end of push day help posture
The push day has no long-head triceps work, which leads to unbalanced arms since the long head is the biggest part; swap pressdowns for overhead cable extensions or skull crushers
A dumbbell press at 10-12 reps is volume, not strength work; intermediates to advanced lifters may need lower reps there
He would never prescribe that much isolation to a novice; novices should focus on compounds and shorter sessions
Separating the bench and the dumbbell press with the incline fly is smart because it rests the shoulders
The incline fly could be supersetted with chin-ups, and the lateral raises, pressdowns and face pulls run as a giant set to save time
Push day lacks ab and calf work; add some
Lat pre-activation sets add no hypertrophy and can be cut; feeling the lats is a matter of form: tuck in, retract the scapula and pull with the back
Prefer pull-ups, then weighted pull-ups, over lat pulldowns; pulldowns are fine but should never be the main strength lift or open the workout
Going from bodyweight to weighted pull-ups makes it hard to match RPE targets with progressive overload
For about 90 percent of people a pull day should open with a pull from the floor (sumo, conventional, Jefferson, behind-the-back or block pulls) to warm up the whole body
Weighted pull-ups after deadlifts help decompress the spine
A third vertical pull and fourth back movement (the omni-grip pulldown) is too much; cut it and focus on progression
Face pulls, reverse pec deck and band pull-aparts are low-impact and can be supersetted with almost anything
EZ-bar curl 3x6-8 is a rare intense biceps prescription and a great way to curl strictly
He strongly dislikes the incline dumbbell curl
Reworked pull day: deadlift 1x5, pull-ups, Meadows rows supersetted with face pulls, EZ curls supersetted with triceps, calves or abs, optional bodyweight chin-ups as a finisher
Squat 3x4-6 then RDL 3x8 is a great pairing; he would widen the RDL to 3x8-12
Three sets each of squat and RDL instead of four keeps the lower back from getting cooked, which compounds over time
Every leg day he reviews is a squat, a hinge and machines, and that is fine; the squat and the hinge are 90 percent of the gains
Leg extensions give no carryover and can be removed; leg curls are worth keeping because they hit the hamstrings in a way hinges cannot
Calves trained only on leg day means twice a week on a 6-day PPL, which is too little; calves can be hit 4-5 times a week
Seated calf raises on leg day, standing calf raises on pull or upper days
To fit deadlifts in, reorder to legs-push-pull-rest or pull-push-legs-rest, or put a rest day between pull and legs
He finds squats more tiring because of the load, so he prioritizes squat recovery
Overhead press and close-grip bench on push 2 is a great combination
With the program as written you bench with a standard grip only once a week, which is a problem for bench strength; rotate paused bench in for close-grip on alternate push-2 days and do it first
His own tests: opening with a horizontal press leaves him fresher for overhead press than the reverse order
The one-arm overhead triceps extension is the only long-head work in the program, which is not enough; superset it with lateral raises
Shrugs fit anywhere in a PPL; add trap work
A deadlift on pull 1 and another hinge (good morning, RDL, stiff-leg or deficit deadlift) on pull 2
A single unchanging leg day is easier to program around than A/B leg days because its volume and fatigue stay constant
A lat pulldown should not be the strength lift; start pull day with a hinge, then a vertical pull or row
The chest-supported T-bar row hurts his sternum, and after a pulldown there is nothing left to offload from
He learned snatch-grip shrugs from Jeff Nippard and loves them
Pull 2 is the worst day, with too much isolation fluff that heavy rows would cover; trimming it by 40 percent gives better gains
If you can shrink a day, always shrink it
Upper/push days should be the longest, pull days in between and legs the shortest; legs is where shrugs and calves can go
As you progress you must add hard sets, not fluff, which gets hard to balance when supersets are not optimized

chest finisher, may hit upper chest
